lead: Many real forces do not lie in one plane: a cable from a tower, a tripod leg, a corner of a cupboard. In space a force needs three components, not two. The same vector rules still work, but equilibrium now gives three equations and a resultant needs direction cosines. The method builds a force from two points, adds several such forces, and uses the three sums to find unknown forces on a particle. It is the three-dimensional form of the plane resultant and equilibrium you already know.
prereq: You need: vector algebra, resolution and composition, free body diagrams and particle equilibrium.

sections.h3: A three-dimensional frame and direction cosines

blocks.text: Place the origin O at any convenient point. Draw x, y and z axes so that curling the fingers of the right hand from x to y makes the thumb point along z. This is the right-hand rule. The unit vectors along the axes are i, j and k. A point A has coordinates (x₁, y₁, z₁) in metres; B has (x₂, y₂, z₂). The vector from A to B is r = (x₂−x₁)i + (y₂−y₁)j + (z₂−z₁)k. Subtract tail coordinates from head coordinates.
|r| = √(rx² + ry² + rz²),  n̂ = r/|r|,  F = F n̂
blocks.where: rx, ry, rz are the components of r in metres; |r| is the length in metres; n̂ is the unit vector along r; the left F is the force vector in newtons; the right F is its magnitude in newtons.

blocks.text: The components of F are Fx = F cos θx, Fy = F cos θy and Fz = F cos θz. θx is the angle between F and the positive x-axis, and similarly for y and z. The direction cosines are cos θx = rx/|r|, cos θy = ry/|r| and cos θz = rz/|r|. They satisfy cos²θx + cos²θy + cos²θz = 1. A vector from B to A is −r, so reversing the order reverses every component and every direction cosine.

sections.h3: Resultant of concurrent forces in space

blocks.text: Concurrent forces all act at the same particle. Write each force as three components with signs. Add the x components, the y components and the z components separately: Rx = ΣFx, Ry = ΣFy and Rz = ΣFz. The resultant is R = Rx i + Ry j + Rz k. Its magnitude is |R| = √(Rx² + Ry² + Rz²). Its direction cosines are cos θx = Rx/|R|, cos θy = Ry/|R| and cos θz = Rz/|R|. Here θx, θy, θz are the angles between R and the positive axes. The identity cos²θx + cos²θy + cos²θz = 1 is a check. There is no single plane angle for a space force; direction cosines replace it. If the three totals are all zero, the forces have no resultant and the particle is in equilibrium.

items: Write every force from its magnitude and direction cosines, or from two points using n̂.
Add all x components with signs; repeat for y and z.
Compute R and its direction cosines from the three totals.
Check that the squares of the direction cosines add to 1.

sections.h3: Equilibrium of a particle in space

blocks.text: A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces on it is zero. In space this gives three scalar equations: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣFz = 0. Each equation is independent. With known lines of action, these equations can find at most three unknown scalar magnitudes or angles. A cable carries tension along its own line and pulls the particle toward its support (away from the particle, along the cable). A two-force member may push or pull: a strut (compression) pushes, a tie (tension) pulls. Assume a direction, and a negative answer means the opposite direction. Draw a three-dimensional free body diagram first: mark axes, the particle, and every force with its line and assumed arrow. Some syllabi call this 'equilibrium of a particle in space'. Three-dimensional support reactions are not solved here; see Unit 2, Equilibrium of rigid bodies in two and three dimensions.

blocks.where: Fx, Fy, Fz are the x, y, z components of every force on the particle in newtons; the sums include signs.

figure.caption: The flow starts from two points, builds the vector AB, then the unit vector and the force components. The highlighted equilibrium box is where vector equilibrium becomes three scalar equations.

spec.title: From points to equilibrium
spec.aria: A downward flowchart from the coordinates of points A and B, to vector AB, its length and unit vector, the force vector, the three equilibrium sums, and solution of at most three unknowns.

examples.question: A particle at A(1, 2, 0) m is acted on by two forces. F₁ has magnitude 260 N along the line from A to B(4, 6, 12) m. F₂ has magnitude 130 N along the line from A to C(5, −10, 3) m. (a) Write F₁ as a vector and give its direction cosines. (b) Find the resultant R and its magnitude. (c) Find the third force F₃ that keeps the particle in equilibrium, and state its magnitude.
steps: cos θx = 3/13 = 0.231, cos θy = 4/13 = 0.308, cos θz = 12/13 = 0.923. Their squares add to 1.
Equilibrium needs F₁ + F₂ + F₃ = 0, so F₃ = −R = −100i + 40j − 270k N. Its magnitude is the same, 290.7 N.
examples.answer: F₁ = 60i + 80j + 240k N with direction cosines 0.231, 0.308, 0.923; F₂ = 40i − 120j + 30k N; R = 100i − 40j + 270k N of magnitude 290.7 N; and F₃ = −100i + 40j − 270k N of magnitude 290.7 N.
examples.check:
import math
A = (1, 2, 0)
B = (4, 6, 12)
C = (5, -10, 3)
def v(P, Q):
    return (Q[0]-P[0], Q[1]-P[1], Q[2]-P[2])
def m(u):
    return math.sqrt(u[0]**2 + u[1]**2 + u[2]**2)
AB = v(A, B)
AC = v(A, C)
F1 = tuple(260*c/m(AB) for c in AB)
F2 = tuple(130*c/m(AC) for c in AC)
R = tuple(F1[i]+F2[i] for i in range(3))
Rm = m(R)
print(round(F1[0]))
print(round(F1[1]))
print(round(F1[2]))
print(round(AB[0]/m(AB), 3))
print(round(AB[1]/m(AB), 3))
print(round(AB[2]/m(AB), 3))
print(round(F2[0]))
print(round(F2[1]))
print(round(F2[2]))
print(round(R[0]))
print(round(R[1]))
print(round(R[2]))
print(round(Rm, 1))
print(round(-R[0]))
print(round(-R[1]))
print(round(-R[2]))
print(round(Rm, 1))

traps: Using raw coordinates x₂, y₂, z₂ instead of coordinate differences; the vector must start at A.
Forgetting to divide by |AB|, so the force is magnitude times r rather than magnitude times n̂.
Taking the line B to A when the force is stated A to B; reverse order reverses signs.
Adding magnitudes or using one plane angle; space forces add component by component.
Expecting three equilibrium equations to solve four unknown cable tensions.

quiz.q: Write the three scalar equations of equilibrium for a particle in space.
Why do the direction cosines satisfy cos²θx + cos²θy + cos²θz = 1?
quiz.a: They are the components of a unit vector; a unit vector has length 1, so the sum of squared components is 1.

quiz.q: A 50 N force acts from P(1, 0, 2) m to Q(3, 4, 2) m. Write it as a vector.
A particle is pulled by cables along positive x, positive y and positive z axes with tensions 30 N, 40 N and 50 N. What fourth force holds equilibrium?
quiz.a: Resultant of cables is 30i + 40j + 50k N; fourth force = −30i − 40j − 50k N, magnitude 70.7 N.

quiz.q: In a 3D free body diagram, which way does a cable tension on the particle point?
quiz.a: Away from the particle along the cable, because a cable pulls.

quiz.q: A direction has cos θx = 0.4 and cos θy = 0.5. Find the positive cos θz.
A particle has ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, but ΣFz = 12 N. Is it in equilibrium? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Equilibrium requires all three sums zero. The net force is 12 N along z, so the particle accelerates unless another force supplies −12 N along z.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, three-dimensional force balance is the daily tool of riggers, crane planners and spacecraft engineers: a spreader bar with four slings becomes a particle equilibrium problem when the bar is small compared with the sling lengths, so all slings meet at one point and the bar's own weight is neglected. Finite element software builds the same three equations at every node, then solves thousands of them together. Search for 'space truss analysis', 'cable net structures' or '3D equilibrium particle' to see the next step. The same direction-cosine idea reappears in computer graphics, where a surface normal is a unit vector.
